title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia EditorReporting fromMoscowAfter two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard."In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace."I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said,  "but things are moving in that direction."All rather vague.It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken holdIn recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader."Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says."Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?""Of course!"A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe."Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace

title: Holocaust school lessons to be improved after 'shocking' antisemitism review
description: Education Secretary Lucy Powell says the government will "update and strengthen" Holocaust education within schools after a major review highlighted t
body: Education Secretary Lucy Powell says the government will "update and strengthen" Holocaust education within schools after a major review highlighted the "shocking scale" of antisemitism in British society.Schools and colleges in England will be required to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it.It means anti-Jewish hatred will be treated as a specific safeguarding risk rather than being dealt with through existing measures to stop racism and bullying.The government has accepted all of the 27 recommendations made in the government-commissioned review including dedicated training for teachers and more consistent recording of incidents.The review into antisemitism in schools and colleges in England was led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell and presented to Parliament on Wednesday. Powell told the BBC it marked a "generational moment" to re-educate young people, among whom she said the issue of antisemitism was "particularly prevalent".She said: "It's definitely a crisis and I think it's actually got worse since Sir David began this review. This has become a real challenge for Jewish people in our country, but also Jewish students and Jewish teachers working in our schools and colleges."I do really feel it is a generational moment to educate this generation and the next – that is the job of education – to understand what antisemitism is in the modern world."Speaking on Holocaust education, the education secretary said new lessons will "challenge" some of the concepts that young people have. The review also calls for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers.Powell told the House of Commons "teachers should not bring their own political views into the classroom" but they should not avoid discussing important topics.The review was launched following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025, in which two men were killed.Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws.The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse.It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters.The review also recommends that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism.Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.He told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries."Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role."When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said. "We think about it a lot."In response to the recommendations, the government will also encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."Rabbi Charley Baginksy and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leads of the Movement for Progressive Judaism, said that the report "exposes serious failures in how schools recognise and respond to antisemitism".They said:  "Alongside that urgent question of how schools deal with hatred and educate about Jewish persecution, we also need to ensure they teach about Jewish creativity, music, literature, humour and the extraordinary pleasure of belonging to this diverse tradition."Dan Green, Chief Executive of the Anne Frank Trust UK, said the review "confirms what we see in classrooms every day"."Antisemitism in our schools is real, it is widespread, and too often it goes unrecognised and unchallenged.""One-off assemblies are not enough, and neither is sitting pupils in front of a video. Young people need the space to ask difficult questions, challenge their own assumptions and understand that antisemitism did not start or end with the Holocaust."The National Education Union raised concerns about creating a "hierarchy of racism" and adopting the IHRA definition.It said the latter risked "blurring the line between antisemitism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government and the genocide in Gaza".The union welcomed a "strengthened focus on antisemitism" while underlining that "no form of racism should be minimised".Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.It found in the first half of 2026 that antisemitism in schools had reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year.

schema.headline: Holocaust school lessons to be improved after 'shocking' antisemitism review

title: Glee reboot: The US high school musical comedy-drama is to return on Hulu and Disney+
description: We never stopped believin'... now it's official: Glee, the Emmy-winning US high school musical comedy drama, is set to return.Ryan Murphy's series, wh
body: We never stopped believin'... now it's official: Glee, the Emmy-winning US high school musical comedy drama, is set to return.Ryan Murphy's series, which chronicled the highs and lows of choir members from Ohio, premiered on Fox in 2009 and ran for six seasons until 2015.The original cast included Lea Michele, Amber Riley, the late Cory Monteith, Jane Lynch and Matthew Morrison as Will Schuester, the optimistic teacher leading the fictional McKinley High's glee club.The reboot was announced, external by Disney and Hulu via the show's social media team on Wednesday.The show was a huge hit first time around, known for its big laughs and big heart, tackling topics such as sexuality, race, disability and mental health.In the series, glee club New Directions helped misfit students find their voices through song and dance.Lynch served as the club's main antagonist, the villainous cheerleading coach Sue Sylvester.The choir's covers of Don't Stop Believin', River Deep, Mountain High and Smooth Criminal also brought older hit songs to the attention of younger audiences.In 2010, the show was adapted for a concert tour in which was captured on film.Around the same time, the cast overtook The Beatles as the non-solo act with the most Billboard Hot 100 appearances.On Wednesday, the Wanted singer Max George told BBC Scotland that appearing in the show's sixth season was "an amazing experience", adding that he'd "love to do it again"."I messaged the casting director from it, just with wide eyes from the announcement," he said. Asked if it makes sense for the series to come back, he said: "I think so… It's been over 10 years, so I think that's a nice break. "I think it was probably coming towards the end in terms of the storylines and everything, but 10 years has gone by, and Ryan Murphy will probably come up with something genius. So I'm expecting big things."In a recent interview with Entertainment Tonight, co-creator Murphy confirmed he had written a reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan.He also said he had "been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members"."It's very sweet, they all had a lot of questions but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea," he said. "Nobody's read it, so we'll see."He added: "I vowed to myself that I wanted to write a couple of them to see what people think, particularly the cast, because we were very close when we were making it."It came after Michelle, who played Rachel Berry, the ambitious singer at the centre of the club, had told E! News that she - like Lynch - would be more than happy to return."I will always love Glee," she said. "I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me... I will follow Ryan wherever he goes."Speaking to Bustle recently, another star of the show, Chris Colfer, admitted that any such reboot would be difficult following the death of Naya Rivera, who played Glee club favourite Santana Lopez."It was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya is gone," said Colfer, who portrayed Kurt Hummel - the flamboyant singer and original choir member who faces bullying at the school."But I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no. So I don't know, but hopefully I'll have more information and I can actually think about it."Rivera died in 2020 at the age of 33 in an accidental drowning.Hers was the third death among the Glee cast. Monteith, who played football star turned singer Finn Hudson, died in 2013 at the age of 31 from a toxic mix of alcohol and heroin.Mark Salling, another Glee cast member, took his own life in 2018 at the age of 35 while awaiting sentencing on child pornography charges.A mini Glee reunion occurred on Sunday at London's Royal Albert Hall, when Darren Criss, aka Glee's Blaine Anderson, brought out Colfer for a duet of the song Baby It's Cold Outside.Earlier this month, former Glee co-stars Harry Shum Jr and Amber Riley reunited on Dancing with the Stars.

schema.headline: Glee reboot: The US high school musical comedy-drama is to return on Hulu and Disney+

title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy
description: Image source, AFP/Getty ImagesImage caption, Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened Number 10 North in JulyByEwan SomervillePolitical reporterA "mindset s
body: Image source, AFP/Getty ImagesImage caption, Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened Number 10 North in JulyByEwan SomervillePolitical reporterA "mindset shift" is needed across the UK's central government to help Number 10 North deliver its objectives, its deputy director has said.Duncan Parish told a conference in Lincolnshire on Wednesday there were "institutional challenges" within government that needed to be overcome to deliver change.The Manchester office of Number 10 North - sister to London's Downing Street - was set up by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July.Burnham's political opponents have called the office a "gimmick" and raised transparency concerns about the costs involved.Speaking to the Great Exhibition conference of local political and business leaders, Parish said his career in the civil service to date had "not been without its frustrations" and there can be "friction" between different parts of government which have "similar but ever so slightly competing objectives".Parish, a civil servant in Whitehall before moving to Manchester four years ago, said Number 10 North staff were "delivering outcomes at a national level across a huge range of areas" including health, transport, education and social care."But we continually need to work to overcome those institutional challenges," he added.He said one priority of Number 10 North was to "shift power and accountability" closer to local areas, but acknowledged "that means reforming the civil service as well" - by not viewing national, regional and local government as separate.Image source, Great Exhibition conferenceImage caption, Duncan Parish spoke to local political and business leaders in Lincolnshire, in an event chaired by regional mayor Dame Andrea JenkynsDescribing Number 10 North's second focus of growth, Parish told local leaders: "We're here to unblock issues that may have become stalled or where boundaries within government end up being a hindrance."He said that "too often, working within government or departments can be perceived as either difficult or slow"."But to deliver that change, requires us all to change - and part of that change is a mindset shift within central government," he said."We need to focus on the whole country and work across those boundaries, bringing in mayoral strategic authorities like Greater Lincolnshire into discussions that previously they may not have been part of - working bottom-up, rather than top-down."His comments come as the government continues to face questions about the cost to the taxpayer of the new headquarters.Few figures releasedIn September, Conservative shadow minister Mike Wood raised concerns about "little information and so little transparency" surrounding Number 10 North which he described as a "gimmick"."The minister either doesn't know or won't tell us how much No 10 North will cost, how many people work there or how many of them actually turn up to work - it's almost as though this hasn't been properly thought through," he told a House of Commons debate.He called for the annual budget, staff levels and office attendance statistics to be published. Current staffing levels have also not yet been clarified.Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson said last week that the government did not know how much has been spent on hotels for No 10 North staff, ministers and special advisers travelling between London and Manchester since it opened.The cost is "not centrally collated" but is "being met within existing departmental budgets", Jameson said in response to a parliamentary question.Number 10 North's latest summit of regional mayors, held in its "situation room", will take place on Thursday. Burnham has previously indicated he will work there at least once a week, and hosted the Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in September.Parish added in his speech: "How will we know if Number 10 North is working?"Ultimately, success will be in people in the UK feeling the difference in their communities, with greater opportunities, improved living standards, faster decisions...more joined up services and a stronger voices in the future of their place."

schema.headline: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

title: MP Henry Tufnell harassed for 'being English' by man who took axe to pub
description: A man who harassed a Labour MP for being "English", and claimed he knew where he lived, has been given a suspended jail sentence.Michael Glover, 59, l
body: A man who harassed a Labour MP for being "English", and claimed he knew where he lived, has been given a suspended jail sentence.Michael Glover, 59, left a note on Mid and South Pembrokeshire MP Henry Tufnell's office door in Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, on 10 March, and carried an axe to the pub the following day.In the letter, which he signed, he also wrote that he had taken "a look around" Tufnell's family home and had "left some presents".The MP said he felt "uneasy" that the defendant said he knew where he lived with his family, including his newborn baby.Swansea Crown Court heard Glover, who is a wheelchair user and has "complex mental health difficulties", was "frustrated" because of a delay in his application for a blue badge.The court heard that CCTV captured the defendant taping a bag, which contained the letter, to the front door of Tufnell's office. He then made "gestures" to the camera before driving away.On 11 March, he carried an axe in a plastic bag to a local pub, and picked it up in front of a member of the public.Glover was arrested that day, and later pleaded guilty to both charges at the magistrates' court.Regan Walters, prosecuting, read a victim personal statement by Tufnell, who said the incident made him feel "uncomfortable"."Knowing that Glover knows where I live with my wife and young child has made me rethink things, such as the security of my address," the politician said.He said he had to be mindful that his "panic alarms and CCTV cameras are working" and that, when he worked away, he felt "on edge, wondering if [his family] are safe".Joseph Hocquard, representing Glover, said his client had been in custody for the past four months for breaching a probation order, which he said had been "incredibly challenging" because of his mental health and disabilities.Glover appeared via video link with his barrister in the cells at Swansea Crown Court because of a "technical issue" with the lift in the building.Judge Mark Powell KC told him "members of parliament are there to advocate for their constituents".He said: "They are entitled to go about their business, without being subject to the sort of threats and harassment that you carried out… regardless of if they are English or not English."He also said that brandishing an axe in public would have been "extremely frightening for those around" but that he "didn't intend to harm anyone".The judge told the court that it was "frustration" and a "deterioration in his mental state" that led to Glover committing the offence. He said he was satisfied the defendant had shown remorse for both offences, and that he needed support and medication for his "complex mental health" needs.Judge Powell gave him a six-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, as well as a five-year restraining order.He was also ordered to pay a victim surcharge of £154.

schema.headline: MP Henry Tufnell harassed for 'being English' by man who took axe to pub

title: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
description: The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do
body: The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent".Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood. He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021.The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs. He told the court that staff and managers at the Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had jobs elsewhere.At the height of the alleged deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector. In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days. Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023.Chowdhury said the jobs were a "lifeline" during a time his mother's health had declined.Asked by defence barrister Pieter Briegel what extent stress in his life was due to the number of jobs, he replied: "The jobs at the time were my lifeline at the time, that was what I survived on at that particular moment."And they gave me a link to the outside, they were the only thing I had to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time," he told the court.The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity". A succession of Chowdhury's line managers have told the jury that he performed poorly in his roles. Abigail Mounde, who was Chowdhury's line manager at the Department for Business and Trade previously told the court: ''Any basic tasks I asked him to do he either did late or not to the standard I would have expected."Chowdhury was asked whether he accepted the criticism of his performance, including the allegation he failed to deliver work on time. He replied: "I reject them all."The prosecution also alleges Chowdhury used sick notes from his doctor as part of the cover-up. But the prosecution said while he was telling some employers he was sick and unfit to work because of "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" he was not giving sick notes to other employers. The prosecution said this ''underlines the dishonesty involved in the whole affair".His line manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, arranged a video call in May 2023, to support him returning to work after a period of absence.In previous evidence she told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin.She told the court that as the call went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ told the court: ''This almost laughable incident demonstrates quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit.''The trial continues.

schema.headline: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs

title: Bruno Fernandes rounds on Michael Carrick after Man Utd lose to Como in Champions League
description: Figure caption, Man Utd humbled by four-goal Como to pile pressure on CarrickByManchester United reporter in ComoManchester United captain Bruno Ferna
body: Figure caption, Man Utd humbled by four-goal Como to pile pressure on CarrickByManchester United reporter in ComoManchester United captain Bruno Fernandes turned on head coach Michael Carrick following one of the most humiliating nights in the club's European history.A 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como led to Carrick fielding questions about his future.He apologised to the 700 travelling fans, having ignored his beaten players after the final whistle to march across the pitch and repeatedly hold his hands up - in a manner similar to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4-1 defeat at Watford in November 2021 which led to his dismissal as United boss 24 hours later.However, Fernandes - widely accepted as a football obsessive who watches games regularly and understands the tactical side as well as any player in the United squad - inflicted more damage when he spoke to TNT Sports afterwards."It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," he said.Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."Told of Fernandes' comments in his post-match press conference, Carrick offered a curt response: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."Figure caption, 'That is on the manager' - Fernandes on Man Utd tacticsCarrick avoids questions on future, apologises to fans for unacceptable displayCarrick also refused to answer questions about his own future.Instead, he described his own feelings about United's performance and focused on taking responsibility."I have to apologise to the supporters," said the former player. "I care about this football club as much as anyone, if not more, with the position that I'm in and what I value this football club. For us to play in that way is not acceptable."I always go over to the fans anyway, regardless, so it wasn't a particularly different kind of reason why I went over."It's the appreciation and acknowledgement of what they've gone through and have done over a period of a few weeks now. As I said, I was one of them."I'm feeling the same as them. We've got a lot of values in this football club; what we represent and how we want to go about it. We might win, we might lose, but the way we went about it tonight wasn't acceptable. I just wanted to let the fans know that I feel for them."Listen. I've not given my own position any thought - this is for the supporters - I was one of them watching that and I wasn't happy all."Figure caption, Carrick responds to Fernandes criticism on tacticsSeven without a win - Man Utd's bleak pictureAfter winning 12 of his 17 games in charge last season to guide United back into the Champions League after a two-year absence, Carrick was given a two-year contract.However, as happened with Solskjaer five years ago, the new campaign has unravelled spectacularly and they are 13th in the Premier League, three points clear of bottom club Sunderland.Although they recovered from their shock opening-day defeat to newly promoted Hull by coming from behind to beat Ipswich the following week, United have not won in the Premier League since. Their only other success in 11 games in all competitions came against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League.Their latest loss meant they have now gone seven games without a win, their worst run since they went eight without a victory under Louis van Gaal between 25 November and 28 December 2015.Only Joshua Zirkzee's injury-time consolation prevented United suffering their joint second-worst European defeat of all time.The embarrassment was heightened by the knowledge that when they were last crowned European champions in 2008, Como were playing semi-professional football in front of a couple of hundred spectators in Serie D.It is a basic reality that if Como's star man Nico Paz, who opened the scoring after 118 seconds, created the second and added a third goal, said he wanted to leave Como, virtually every big club in Europe would want to sign him and United's chances would be virtually non-existent.They entertain 15th-placed Bournemouth in the Premier League on Sunday knowing that prior to last season's amazing 4-4 draw, the Cherries recorded 3-0 wins on their previous two visits to Old Trafford.Figure caption, Carrick 'bitterly disappointed' by Man Utd peformanceWhat happens now?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick acknowledges the club's fans after the 4-1 defeat by ComoUnited flew straight back to Manchester after the game.It remains to be seen whether the position around Carrick changes before the Bournemouth game. However, United supporters sang against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe as the shambolic evening unravelled. Both Carrick and sporting director Jason Wilcox have been absolved of partial blame for the club's plight by some; Carrick because he was let down badly in the summer transfer window, when the club signed three midfielders, but failed to bring in competition for Luke Shaw at left-back and Benjamin Sesko in attack. Wilcox too, because he had to work to a budget set by those above him, including chief executive Omar Berrada."There was a lot going through my mind watching that," admitted Carrick, who won five Premier League titles and the Champions League during his United playing career. "It was tough to watch."It wasn't just the goals, if I'm totally honest. It was was the manner and way we played at times."I'm giving my absolute best all the time, I care about it. My whole life is wrapped around it. It might go well, it might not go so well, but I I genuinely give everything that I possibly can."Figure caption, Man Utd fans on if Carrick should stayFollow Manchester United on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical United contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about the Red Devils

schema.headline: Bruno Fernandes rounds on Michael Carrick after Man Utd lose to Como in Champions League

title: Jackdaw: Will it cut energy bills and how much gas will it provide?
description: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has said the gas from Jackdaw "won't lower energy bills this winter".And most energy analysts do not expect the add
body: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has said the gas from Jackdaw "won't lower energy bills this winter".And most energy analysts do not expect the additional gas production from Jackdaw to have a significant, direct impact on households' energy bills, either.This is because of the way natural gas markets work. Great Britain is integrated with wider European gas markets and physically linked to the continent through undersea pipelines.Gas prices faced by British households and businesses are effectively set at a pan-European level and determined by the price customers across Europe are prepared to pay for the energy.People across the continent have seen their energy bills rise significantly in recent years, fuelled by the wars in Ukraine and Iran affecting gas and oil supplies.But the additional gas being pumped into the UK's system from Jackdaw will still be relatively small, and unlikely to significantly move the European price paid by British firms and households."Essentially, producing more British energy doesn't necessarily mean cheaper British energy," Karl Matikonis, professor of taxation at University College Dublin, told BBC Verify."North Sea oil and gas are sold at market prices rather than reserved for British consumers at a discount."The enviromental impact of Jackdaw has also been a significant point of contention. Advocates argue the gas field would be beneficial because the carbon emissions arising from production from the the UK's own North Sea field will be lower than those arising from the production of US LNG.The North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the sector, has estimated the emissions arising from the production, delivery and processing of US LNG are around three times higher than from the production of North Sea natural gas.That is because the process of liquefying, shipping and then turning LNG back in to natural gas on arrival is extremely energy intensive, compared with pumping it ashore by a pipeline, creating higher carbon emissions.However, NSTA estimates that Norwegian North Sea gas production - which Britain already imports by pipeline in large volumes - has a considerably lower average emissions impact than that of the UK's existing North Sea gas production.This is because UK North Sea gas mostly comes from smaller fields and is extracted with older infrastructure and technology than those of Norway.The owner of Jackdaw estimates the emissions intensity, external of its production would be lower than from older UK North Sea infrastructure - though it would still be higher than gas produced from Norwegian fields.So the impact on the environment of the Jackdaw decision partly depends on what happens to the mix of UK gas consumption in future - and where it comes from - which is uncertain.If additional gas production from Jackdaw displaces US LNG imports, UK-related national emissions could be lower than otherwise.But if additional gas production from Jackdaw displaces gas imports from Norway instead then UK-related national emissions could be higher than otherwise.

schema.headline: Jackdaw: Will it cut energy bills and how much gas will it provide?

title: Andy Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.These are fixed daily fees that cover the
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used.Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill.But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock £27 off a typical annual bill.During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity".No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firm Nesta that they could be moved to the unit rate, external, so people pay for what they use.This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more. For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges.Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers.Average standing charges are 54.8p a day for electricity and 29.7p a day for gas.When asked why electricity standing charges would not be scrapped as well, the PM's official spokesman said VAT had already been cut on electricity bills.Standing charges cover costs such as transporting energy to homes via pipes and wires, and the upkeep of that infrastructure.The standing charges also fund schemes to support low-income households.Many of these costs will need to be recouped somehow, but Citizens Advice has warned, external about the potential consequences of reform for vulnerable customers.Vulnerable people who don't have a high income, but have high energy usage, could be penalised.But Madeleine Gabriel, director of sustainable future at Nesta, said: "Abolishing the gas standing charge and moving those costs onto the unit rate would help those worst hit by rising energy prices."Pressure remains on the chancellor to offer more fundamental, targeted energy support this winter in his Budget next week, with energy prices forecast to rise by 16% to a four-year high in January.In addition to standing charges, Burnham said investing in renewables would also bring household bills down "substantially" by breaking the link between gas and electricity prices "in this parliament".Electricity prices in the UK are mainly set by gas prices, and this is often cited as a reason why electricity prices in the UK are higher than many other countries.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills

title: Helen Haines: 'Targeted' attack on much-loved Australian MP leaves Wangaratta heartbroken
description: Wangaratta has been thrust into an unwelcome spotlight this week. Residents in this rural Victorian town are used to catering to tourists passing thro
body: Wangaratta has been thrust into an unwelcome spotlight this week. Residents in this rural Victorian town are used to catering to tourists passing through on their way to regional wineries, or music lovers visiting its annual jazz and blues festival.Instead, locals are fielding endless questions about their MP - and having to explain to strangers what it all means for the town's nearly 30,000 people.They are clearly in shock about what police say was a targeted and deliberate attack on Helen Haines on Monday afternoon, when she was struck by a car just outside her office."People are simply dumbfounded and finding it very hard to fathom the scale of this tragedy," Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who represents King Charles, said at a press conference on Wednesday.The independent federal MP had to have both legs amputated after she was airlifted to Melbourne. But the "two most important parts of Helen", her heart and her mind, were in "good shape", her husband Phil Haines said.The MP isn't a divisive figure, locals tell the BBC, and no one can understand why she was allegedly targeted."Everyone knows Helen," says Jane Hill, who owns a giftware shop a few hundred metres down the town's main street from where Haines was hit."She is a such a good person in our community. She'd go to everything - celebrations, funerals, she's one of those genuinely kind people - and so are her family."Local man Brendan Nugent, whose father has been good friends with Haines for decades, faces at least three charges over the alleged attack including intentionally causing harm and appeared in court on Wednesday. Police say they are considering further charges, including attempted murder.First elected to parliament in 2019, Haines is best known for her years-long efforts to establish a national anti-corruption commission.She was spurred on by a series of major political scandals which, in her words, saw "public money spent for political gain", disproportionate spending on "shiny infrastructure projects" in marginal seats and decisions benefitting big donors over ordinary people.The commission finally opened in 2023 under Anthony Albanese's Labor government.Haines has also helped to secure funds for housebuilding, railway improvements and health infrastructure in her region, which she argues has long been sidelined by policies favouring cities.On a spring afternoon in Wangaratta, nobody seemed to have a bad word to say about the former nurse and midwife turned politician.Local Mayor Irene Grant described her as "warm", "cheerful" and "committed", and pointed to her record on climate action and Indigenous rights.In a police update on Wednesday, Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush said she'd given "wonderful support" to local police when two officers were shot dead in the nearby town of Porepunkah last year.Bystanders who came to Haines' aid recalled how she thanked them even as she lay severely injured."It was incredible," Jacklyn Black told Nine Network's Today show. "We were having conversations, she was telling me about her grandkids.""To be in that situation and be as calm as she could be in the moment, but also thankful to the aid that the community had given her... I could [not] speak any more highly of her in a moment like that," Cody Lepoidevin added."She just thanked everyone."There's a large print-out of Helen Haines plastered onto the window of her office - anyone delivering flowers for her gets a big smile back as they look up and walk away.Across the road on Tuesday, a man waved an Australian flag. On his T-shirt were the words "Wangaratta - this is not us!!"It's clear that many feel that way in this friendly community where people look out for each other.Next door to Haines' office is RickyChops barbershop, owned by Ricky Jefferies. When he heard the chaos unfolding outside, he rushed to help, pinning down the suspect."I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him, and I told him that he can't leave," he explained after the incident."I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way."Some clearly disagree with Ricky. By Tuesday afternoon, he too had received a bouquet of flowers tied to his shop's door, and a small balloon with the words "thank you".Down the road at the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral, a vigil was held, attended by a couple of hundred people lining up to light a candle for Haines.Some hugged the clergy, while others wore campaign T-shirts carrying the words "Team Helen Haines".Her husband Phil said he had received "thousands upon thousands" of messages of love and support."I can only say how much of a difference that makes to all of us," he said. "Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter.""Whether you vote for her or not, she seems to have the community at heart so that's all you can really ask for; a politician that represents your community," said Austin Longfield who lives in nearby Albury."It's just something that you wouldn't expect in our community," he added. "You see it in other countries and it's just something that I didn't comprehend could happen here."With additional reporting by Simon Atkinson

schema.headline: Helen Haines: 'Targeted' attack on much-loved Australian MP leaves Wangaratta heartbroken

title: Google staff resign in backlash over its AI contracts with military
description: Google is facing a backlash from some staff members over the company's deployment of its AI technology for military use.The BBC has spoken to several
body: Google is facing a backlash from some staff members over the company's deployment of its AI technology for military use.The BBC has spoken to several tech workers who have either recently resigned from Google's AI company, Google DeepMind, or are in the process of leaving, over concerns with the tech firm's military contracts.Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer, is one of them. She resigned from Google DeepMind this week and spoke about her concerns exclusively with the BBC, despite her contract restricting her from doing so."Realising my company is pushing more and more for AI systems in military operations makes me feel ashamed to work at Google," Liguori said, speaking in a personal capacity.In response, a Google spokesperson told the BBC: "We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles.""We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns - ranging from business ethics to misconduct - and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind."Google is one of several tech companies that signed contracts with the US military earlier this year to deploy AI across classified military environments. The US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has made integrating AI into the armed forces a key priority, saying the Trump administration will become an "AI-first warfighting force".But AI technology is evolving rapidly, and critics question whether it is reliable enough to be used in warfare without more testing, stronger guardrails and human oversight.After working for the company for three years, Liguori said she decided to resign over Google's increasing work with the US and Israeli militaries. "I don't agree with this direction and this has led me to lose faith in my company being true to its stated ethical values," she said.Those values, according to Google's AI Principles, external, include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning the technology with "international law and human rights". But former and current staff at the company, and experts the BBC spoke to, said they were concerned about the level of human oversight at critical moments.In the past few years, the US military has deployed multiple AI-enabled technologies to help advance its warfighting abilities.The most prominent example of this is Maven Smart Systems, the Pentagon's main software platform for organising intelligence and data.Developed by US defence company Palantir, it uses AI to help personnel select and identify targets to strike. Palantir has integrated the technology from several leading AI companies into Maven, and it has enabled some processes to be significantly speeded up.Retired Lieutenant General Jack Shanahan, who is the former director of Project Maven, said the "philosophy" seems to be: "Go as fast as possible to deploy [AI technology] as widely as possible, potentially at the expense of the rigour and discipline of test and evaluation."However, the Pentagon has maintained that adopting AI technologies is essential for winning wars. "Speed defines victory in the AI era," said Emil Michael, an under secretary in the US Department of Defense, in a statement earlier this year.Google's contract with the Pentagon, which was signed earlier this year, allows its AI technology to be used for classified military work. The agreement says Google's AI models can be used for "any lawful government purpose" and "should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weapons (including target selection) without appropriate human oversight and control".Similar contracts were signed by OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia, and the start-up Reflection, to allow AI technology to be deployed across a range of military settings such as transport, planning and battlefield operations. As the tech quickly evolves, concerns are growing about the use of AI in theatres of war."AI compresses the time an operator has to make a decision because it works much faster than a person, and that's especially risky in a high-stress environment," said Sarah Shoker, formerly head of OpenAI's Geopolitics team."When you have hundreds of targets that are selected by AI and a short amount of time, it is almost impossible for a human operator to meaningfully review the AI's outputs for errors."Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticising the company."In principle I'm not allowed to criticise Google for the duration of my life," Sofia Liguori told the BBC. But she decided to do so "because I believe it's important for these things to be known and I also think that talking about facts is not criticising".Liguori added that at Google "people are scared of retaliation and putting their career at risk. You feel you are being watched, you can't speak."A current employee at Google DeepMind, who declined to be named for fear of retaliation, told the BBC that "a lot of motivated employees who signed up for [the company's] original mission could leave – but there's also a pipeline of people at the start of the careers who could fill those positions. It could be a changing of the guard."Another Google DeepMind staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC: "A lot of people have left the company that feel strongly about this [how Google DeepMind has changed its ethics position].""Some people are putting up a fight, others are thinking: 'it's a big company. What do you expect to change?'", the employee said.Google's agreements with Israel have also caused controversy. In 2024, the company was criticised by staff for a joint contract with Amazon worth $1.2bn (£960m) called Project Nimbus which provides Israel's government and military with AI technology and cloud computing infrastructure. At the time, Google said Project Nimbus "is not directed at highly sensitive, classified, or military workloads relevant to weapons or intelligence services".Moreover, Israel's AI capabilities in warfare have been the focus of debate after they were featured in a recent documentary, Naza, which examines the role of AI-powered targeting systems to bombard the Gaza Strip, resulting in high civilian casualties. An Israeli government minister has said the claims presented in the film were false and distorted.Former Google employee Andreas Kirsch believes AI technology in warfare is not ready for the battlefield. "Current AI models are not robust enough, and I don't think they have been trained for such tasks either," he said.Additional reporting by Rosa Rahimi

schema.headline: Google staff resign in backlash over its AI contracts with military

title: Ali G is back. But is Sacha Baron Cohen's character past its sell-by date?
description: "This is the biggest gathering of cultural appropriators in history," Sacha Baron Cohen tells the camera in his parody of a street accent.Behind him,
body: "This is the biggest gathering of cultural appropriators in history," Sacha Baron Cohen tells the camera in his parody of a street accent.Behind him, hundreds of fans cram onto a London Underground escalator, all wearing Ali G's trademark yellow shell suit and skullcap. Baron Cohen shouts the character's catchphrases through a megaphone, with the crowd enthusiastically finishing each one.Earlier this month, more than 300 fans attended an official Ali G lookalike competition, ferried around London on an open-top bus that stopped at landmarks including Big Ben, Leicester Square and Covent Garden.The stunt was promotion for an upcoming sequel to 2002 film Ali G Indahouse - called Ali G: Who iz I? - which hits cinemas on Friday.But not everyone is excited about the return of Baron Cohen's comedy character. Critics have long accused the actor of perpetuating racial stereotypes with Ali G, and criticism of the upcoming sequel has gained traction online, with social media posts from comedians, content creators and film fans attracting thousands of likes and comments. Among them is singer and presenter Jordan Stephens, who has posted multiple TikToks criticising the franchise's return.And last month, discussing the film's trailer on the Jeremy Vine show, Labour MP Paulette Hamilton called the character racist. She said she believed Baron Cohen would not get away with portraying any other racial group "in the way he has done with the black community". The character of Ali G rose to fame through a series of deadpan TV interviews with figures including Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed and the Beckhams, from which catchphrases such as "Booyakasha" and "Is it because I is black?" entered popular culture.But some critics say these catchphrases have since been appropriated by others in a real-life context to mock black people and dismiss their concerns.Comedian Dane Baptiste, the first black British comic nominated for an Edinburgh Comedy Award, remembers hearing Ali G catchphrases everywhere during the character's noughties heyday. "A lot of the time, I would hear people using phrases like 'Is it because I is black?' or 'Booyakasha'," he recalls."Even taking the phrase 'Is it because I is black?'... that was used to the point of caricature, whereby, whenever black people experienced actual grievances relating to systemic and institutional racism, it was reduced to this catchphrase."Baptiste believes the character, which he calls a "black caricature", is returning at a time when black creatives are being "starved of opportunities". When Ali G first arrived on our screens, characters like him were far more common, says social psychologist Amy Kean. She argues they are no longer "culturally relevant"."Ali G, Little Britain, Catherine Tate, all of those comedians and sketch shows, they made the voice the joke," says Kean, who has written on accentism, drawing from her experiences being teased for her Essex accent."I remember going to school in the 90s and people would take the piss out of anyone whose voice wasn't exactly the same as everyone else's."Baron Cohen has in the past suggested that his character had a knack for pushing powerful interviewees into uncomfortable territory by playing with biases and expectations. Speaking on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert in 2020, Baron Cohen reflected on interviewing Donald Trump for Da Ali G Show, and recalled how the programme's producer was a well-spoken Englishman who Trump had assumed would be conducting the interview."I remember Donald Trump looking at me, and I'm wearing a sweatsuit," Baron Cohen said. "His face dropped. He was immediately furious that he was going to have to speak to somebody from a lower-class borough rather than this rather astute Etonian producer."When discussing the forthcoming sequel on CBS on Tuesday, Baron Cohen's "primary objective" appeared less ideological - to "get people to laugh really hard". Though he added that "smuggled in there is a bit of satire".In a new essay in Time this week, external, Baron Cohen argued that his characters have always been "vehicles to expose prejudice, bias, and stupidity", and that in the case of Ali G, "the joke is on him, and on the predominantly white male establishment" he aims to expose."The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him," Baron Cohen wrote."The world he's returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago. All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven't just lingered - they've metastasized. They're fueled by the greatest propaganda machine in history - social media - and now by its monstrous child, AI."The actor is no stranger to putting himself in potentially dangerous situations for his comedy. In a previous film, he infiltrated a gun rally, disguised as a "right-wing singer", while secretly wearing a bulletproof vest. Once members of the crowd realised they were being mocked, Baron Cohen was escorted into a getaway vehicle as an angry crowd "started pounding on the vehicle with their fists".Judging by Baron Cohen's description of the upcoming film, there may be further potential for danger. He told CBS he wanted to examine "conspiracies and lies" and test whether "we, in a matter of hours, could turn intelligent people who believed in the theory of race replacement into murderers".Colton Dunn, one of the film's black writers, questioned why Baron Cohen would put himself in danger, where interview subjects might react violently, if his intentions were racist. "From my point of view, Ali G is not a racist character. Ali G is a tool to expose racists," Dunn told Deadline."That's why I signed on. I wouldn't sign on to work with somebody that I thought was racist, that's against everything that I've done," he added.Almost 25 years on, Ali G still has loyal fans - including in his "home town" of Staines, in Surrey.Staines-upon-Thames resident Alex Balkan, who campaigned for a statue of Ali G in the town, says the character remains a source of local pride.While acknowledging not everyone welcomes the proposal, he says Ali G put Staines on the map."Everyone knows about us because of Ali G, and many of us wear that as a badge of pride," he says.  "It's a great conversation starter. It feels nice that people know about your town."Asked about accusations of racial stereotyping, Balkan believes the character is designed to be seen as a white man attempting to put on a stereotypical gangster persona, rather than to poke fun at black culture itself.One of the character's defenders is one of his most famous prank victims, politician Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg. "It is clever, satirical humour which makes the country, and many of us look foolish, and that's no bad thing," Sir Jacob posted on his social media. While some argue that audiences may have moved on from Ali G, supporters of the character contend that objections to his return reflect growing concerns about creative freedom in comedy. Balkan goes further, arguing that people today are more easily offended than they were two decades ago."This excessive zeal of political correctness, of left-wing po-facery, is crazy," Sir Jacob said. "It's a joke, it's comedy and it is poking fun at society as it is, as the best comedy often does."It would be unwise to judge the film before audiences have seen it. But the controversy surrounding its release suggests that, more than two decades after Ali G first appeared, the debate over who exactly is being laughed at is far from settled.

schema.headline: Ali G is back. But is Sacha Baron Cohen's character past its sell-by date?

title: Masked boy guilty of trying to murder schoolgirl in Norfolk
description: Teenage boy guilty of trying to murder girl, 15, in schoolImage source, Shaun Whitmore/BBCImage caption, Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School
body: Teenage boy guilty of trying to murder girl, 15, in schoolImage source, Shaun Whitmore/BBCImage caption, Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School at 10:24 GMT on the Wednesday of the attackByRobby Westat King's Lynn Crown Court and Lewis AdamsUpdated 7 hours agoA teenage boy who had a hatred of women and an "obsessive interest" in killers has been found guilty of the attempted murder of a girl at his school.The boy dressed in black and wore a face mask before stabbing the 15-year-old victim in the back at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, in March.Armed police were called to the school, which went into lockdown, and the attack was caught on CCTV.The boy, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, wrote notes about hating women and had an "obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing", jurors at King's Lynn Crown Court were told. He will be sentenced on 18 December.Jurors deliberated for just under four hours before delivering a majority verdict at the end of a trial which began two weeks ago.The teenager "went to school not to learn, but to kill" while armed with a kitchen knife, the prosecution said.The school went into lockdown after the attack and there was an armed police response, while the girl was taken to hospital with a minor injury.Image source, ContributedImage caption, A photo taken from within a classroom showed an armed police officer at the sceneCCTV footage captured the moment the girl was stabbed in the back, before her attacker ran off while "pursued by a teacher".The victim described to the jury how, in the aftermath of the attack, she had told a teacher "Sir, I've been stabbed".In a police interview played to the court, the girl said she was in "panic mode" and felt numb and weak.Chris Paxton KC, prosecuting, said it was "sheer good fortune" the "defenceless and vulnerable" pupil was not seriously hurt."This was a knife strike delivered, we the prosecution say, as an attempt to kill," he added.He messaged his mother to say "I'm sorry" shortly after the attack, jurors heard."I was in complete shock," she told the court.Image source, CPSImage caption, The kitchen knife used to stab the victim had a blade measuring 18cm (7in) and was found in a wooded areaPaxton said that in a note written before the attack, the would-be killer had written: "I really want to do it, really bad, I hate having to wait."The note continued: "Motive = misanthropy, misogyny, suicide, bullying. Weapon = knife x2? Death = 2+ hopefully, injuries a lot hopefully."Jurors heard he had a hatred of women and an "obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing".The boy, who was 15 at the time, had pleaded guilty to possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent, but prosecutors proceeded with the attempted murder charge.The boy did not give evidence during his trial. Instead, his barrister argued he could not have intended to kill the girl because he used "limited force" with the blade.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Pictures shared with the BBC showed some children hiding underneath their desks in the aftermath of the attackAfter the boy was found guilty, the judge Mr Justice Lickley warned him: "I'm sure you understand because of the very serious nature of the offence I will have to consider not only a custodial sentence, but one of some considerable length." He nodded and replied "yes sir" before being led to the cells.Det Supt Andy Hill, of Norfolk Police, said the incident was "unthinkable" and praised the victim's bravery in giving evidence."The resilience shown by the people involved has been truly something remarkable. This has had a deep impact on a lot of people," he said.Owen Jenkins, chief executive of the Broad Horizons Education Trust, added: "We welcome today's guilty verdict, which reflects the seriousness of this shocking and deeply distressing attack. "Incidents of this nature are extremely rare in schools, and our thoughts remain firmly with the student who was attacked and their family."Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Masked boy guilty of trying to murder schoolgirl in Norfolk

title: Lawyer caught by BBC offering to make illegal-worker fine go away
description: A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a £45,000 illegal-working fine go away.Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known
body: A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a £45,000 illegal-working fine go away.Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine, if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.Alias has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office. At least £150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures obtained by the BBC.In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.In a statement, she said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".Many business owners do not take the fines seriously, a law enforcement official has told us anonymously.She told us she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth £40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.When she had asked a member of staff if the business owners intended to pay, she said she had been told: "'It's got nothing to do with me.'"Alias came to our attention during a wider BBC probe into illegal working and criminality linked to some High Street businesses, including mini-marts and barbershops.His name was mentioned in social media videos, including on Kurdish Facebook pages, where business owners in the UK praised his ability to resolve problems linked to immigration fines.For months we monitored these videos, which carried Alias's name, that of his law firm, Liberty Solicitors, and a mobile phone number. Some had more than 20,000 views.In one, a Kurdish-speaking shop owner explained that, after having been issued with a penalty for employing an illegal worker, he had "tried two or three different places to get it sorted but nobody could resolve it".He went on to say that "Mr Alias" had got the fine cancelled - showing a letter as evidence.Alias told the BBC he had not commissioned, paid for, approved or circulated videos on social media.Watch the full film of Ed Thomas's investigation here, externalOur reporter contacted Alias on the phone, claiming to be a business owner who faced a fine after immigration officers had found somebody working at his mini-mart illegally.There was no actual shop, worker, or fine.During the call, which we recorded, Alias told our reporter his services would cost 10% of the fine - in this case, £4,500 - and he would want money up front.Alias explained how liability for the fine could be shifted to somebody outside the UK, if that person could be named as owner of the business."Do you have anybody's name who we can use? Anybody who's gone back to Iraq, gone back to Iran?" he asked.He then offered a fictitious example: "Say we put forward Karwan, yeah? Then fine come on Karwan's name. Karwan not here, Karwan in Iraq."What Alias appeared to be proposing was the use of a "ghost director" - in other words, someone who is paid to put their name on official documents, thereby masking the real owner of a business.Using ghost directors is a widespread illegal practice, the law enforcement official told us.Fitted with a secret camera, our reporter went to Alias's office in Bradford with £250 as an upfront payment.Alias seemed annoyed, having originally asked for £500, and made a show of counting out the notes, but did not provide a receipt.Our reporter had by this time told Alias he had found someone in the Kurdish Region of Iraq ready to declare they were the owner of the mini-mart business.From Alias's office, the reporter rang this supposed contact, a man who gave his name as Saman. In reality, Saman was another BBC undercover journalist based in the UK.As a solicitor, Alias could only ethically argue the case for transferring the fine if Saman were to declare to him, either verbally or in writing, that he was the real owner of the business.In our secret recording of their conversation, Alias repeatedly asks Saman to confirm this, despite knowing there is a question mark over the mini-mart's true ownership.Alias's frustration appears to mount with each attempt.Alias: "Am I right in thinking that you are the owner of the shop and I'm going to write to them explaining that you're the owner of the shop?"Saman: "I'm not the owner of the shop, but I'm ready to transfer it to my name."Alias: "OK, but I'm going to be writing to them [the authorities] to explain that you're the owner of the shop."Saman: "I am happy to do that yeah but also you do know, I am not the owner of the shop? And I've not even seen this shop before!"Alias: "If you're saying that to me, then I can't do that. You understand? I can only do it if you're telling me, you are the owner of the shop."Alias then tries to reassure Saman, telling him: "They might say, 'OK, you have to pay this money.' We don't pay the money. That's the end of it. Case finished."Asked if he has handled similar cases, Alias tells Saman he does it "all the time for people who get fines".Later, Alias sent the undercover reporter a series of messages appearing to withdraw his offer of help.In a subsequent phone call, he repeated that he would not pursue an untruthful claim and said he would arrange for the £250 down payment to be repaid.The money has still not been returned, but Alias says Liberty Solicitors has made numerous attempts to return the cash.Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told us the new review into the illegal-working fines scheme would aim "to ensure we are able to respond to non-compliance and non-payment through all available means".Alias has denied ever advising anyone to put a penalty into the name of someone who was not responsible for a business, or to give false information to the Home Office, and said he never would."My work is to challenge penalties lawfully, through the routes Parliament has provided, usually on the basis that the person found was not an employee at all," Alias told the BBC.He added that when our reporter proposed putting his business into someone else's name, Alias had told him in writing he could not advance an untruthful or dishonest case and did not act for him.

schema.headline: Lawyer caught by BBC offering to make illegal-worker fine go away

body: Depending on the contract you have, data charges may apply for accessing the internet on your mobile device.If you are not sure about the potential charges, please ask your mobile network provider.
